Well, a big disappointment. As a movie that is surreal, this movie could've been great (as high as it is rated by people here), except for the poor acting (director and relatives playing the roles, due to financial reasons, probably) found in here. The title, however, is not only a play of the word, but also giving it a new meaning. A whole new meaning! Anyway, if you are into surreal movies (there are some people who do, actually, like the Japanese movie Circus of Life), you will find a lot of interesting things (and some things) in this movie. There are great visuals here, after all! There are metaphors and ambiguous scenes, but (seeing this movie with a group of friends) almost all of the audience just couldn't stop laughing ... not the intention of the director, probably! Well, everyone has their own taste, as one can see from the high rating of this movie, but I would only recommend this movie if you are aware of the work of Alejandro Jodorowsky's, and/or are into surreal movies.

I've read the book 'Scarlett' and was expecting a good movie the first time I saw it. I'm afraid to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made many changes that I did not like. One of the changes that I did not like the way that Lord Fenton was portrayed. It made no sense to make him out to be a bad man. The way that things ended between Lord Fenton and Scarlett was a lot different and their whole relationship was too intimate. There was also a lot less confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie than was originally written in the book. The movie sent the two in two completely opposite ways and they did not seem to cross paths often enough to make it seem like there still could be love between the two. I've read the book 'Scarlett' and was expecting a great movie adaptation this time around. However, I'm afraid to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made some changes that I did not like. One of them was that I did not like the way that Ashley Fenton was portrayed. It made it seem like Rhett out to be a better man. The way that things played out between Scarlett and Rhett was a bit much and their whole relationship was too intimate. There was also a lot less confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie than what was written in the book. The movie sent the two in two completely different ways and they didn't seem to confront each other enough to make it seem like a connection could be made between the two. A fine movie, but I believe that it really could've been better if it was a little bit more true to Alexandra Rippley's book

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a failed Swedish book editor who decides to take a non-stop train to Berlin. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his mistress scheming to murder the man's wife (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, two gay elderly gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two nuns, a bunch of refugees, and even more people. Meant as a mix of noir-ish thriller (which it does quite well - at least to begin with), and comedy, the film fails with both. It doesn't sit right as the film changes tone with every new scene. And as the train races towards its final destination, the film turns more and more bizarre, ending on a truly surreal note. The good bits are wasted in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It feels like the filmmakers rang everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad that the performances are just as bad as the script (act your lines - don't read them!). The comedy is more or less slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pace is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually) with on scene in particular dragging on for about ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to think that swearing is a good way to replace decent dialogue. The film looks great though, in moody B&W, but it's wasted on such inept film-making in every other department. [1/10]

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a drunken Swedish bookkeeper who decides to take a train to visit his wife. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem wherever he goes. The train also holds a detective, his mistress scheming to murder him, his wife (who's cheating on her husband), a soldier on his way home, two gay English gentlemen, an angry German woman, two nuns, a bunch of kids, and even more people. Meant as a comedic, noir-ish thriller (which it does quite well - at least to begin with), but ultimately, the film fails with everything. It doesn't feel right, the pacing gets worse with every new scene. And as the train heads towards its final destination, the film becomes more and more ridiculous, ending on a very poor note. The good bits are wasted in a myriad of unnecessary plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with great Swedish actors, no matter how small their part is. It's like the filmmakers rang everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad, of course, just don't waste your talent (say your lines - don't read them). The comedy is more or less slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pacing is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually), with on scene in particular dragging on for about ten minutes for no good reason. Most of the film seems to be just exposition, with exposition used to replace decent dialogue. The film looks great though, in its classic B&W, but it's wasted on an inept film, in every other way. [2/5]

I, like most other people, saw this movie after hearing of it from Patton Oswalt. Oddly enough, it was easier to find than I thought it would be. Though, it shouldn't come as a surprise that I found it used. The plot is summed upped masterfully within the title. It's a bed that eats. Nothing more, nothing less. There is an effort to throw in a story line but not a very good one. A demon's blood ended up on a bed and, as a result, it becomes possessed. It devours anything that happens upon it by absorbing and then dissolving it in what appears to be orange Fanta. There is an artist who fell victim to the bed, but was sick and ends up behind a painting in the room it inhabits. The narrative is told entirely through him. This movie fails horribly at everything, even at being bad. Still, it's not without its own brand of charm.

I was curious what other people thought of this movie after I found it on my streaming service. Oddly enough, it was easier to find than I thought it would be. I guess that shouldn't come as a surprise given how obscure it is. This movie is a film that masterfully does almost nothing. It's a bed with demon's blood, more or less. There is barely enough to call it a plot line and not a very interesting one. Even how the demon's blood ended up on the bed is left as a mystery. The movie is a horror film that works by creating a mystery and then dissolving it in what feels like a few seconds. main character is an artist who is drawn to the bed with demon's blood and ends up creating a painting of the room it's in. The narrative is told mostly through dialogue. This movie fails at almost everything, and it's boring. Still, it's not without its own brand of charm.

In this follow-up to The Naked Civil Servant we get the last days of Quentin Crisp's life in New York. John Hurt is again Crisp (who on earth else could play this role?) and its a role he inhabits to the point of disappearing. For me Hurt is the best actor I've seen and it's hard to shake the feeling that Crisp was more interesting than he was himself. Its a great performance. Also great is Denis O'Hare as Phillip Steele, Crisp's long time friend and confidant. Unfortunately, beyond the performances the film has little to recommend it. To be certain the film gets its details right. Filmed in and around New York the way the film looks and talks about New York and its people is accurate, but dramatically its kind of flat. Its Crisp talking about and being himself,trying to come to terms with his life as it began (and ended) in New York, his thoughts concerning his own life, and the infirmities that life has thrust upon him. Crisp's life is always interesting, but his life in general is really not. I am disappointed by this film. I have always admired the man and his unique point of view, and I wish he was better served by this film of his life

Trite and unoriginal. It's like someone watched Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to mix them together and, in the process, steal other formulaic plot parts from other movies to make another one. As with most historical movies nowadays, there are some inaccuracies as history is manipulated to better suit the story, which is understandable for the most part. For example, during the remaining days of Beethoven's life, it was necessary for other people to write down what they needed to say in order for him to understand them. That, of course, would have been a nuisance to have to show on screen. The script, although filled with some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the feel of that time period and, coupled with some bad acting, seems rather contemporary. Diane Kruger is nice enough to look at but she still has lots to improve on her craft. Ed Harris doesn't work for me as Beethoven and I mostly blame Gary Oldman for that. Overall, not a very good interpretation of the musical maestro's life. Better just find yourself a copy of Immortal Beloved. http://iwascalledclementine.multiply.com/reviews

A bland and predictable movie. It's like someone took Immortal Beloved and The Piano Beethoven and decided to mix them together and, in the process, steal some formulaic plot parts from other movies to make this one. As with most historical movies nowadays, there are some inaccuracies as history is subject to change for the sake of the movie to fit the story line. For example, during the last days of Beethoven's life, it was necessary for other people to write down things he needed to say in order for him to understand them. This, of course, would have been a lot of thing to show on screen. The script, while it has some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the feel of the time period and, as with some other movies, seems too contemporary. Diane Keaton is nice enough to look at but she can't carry a movie on her own. Ed Harris was too old to me as Beethoven and I can blame Gary Oldman for that. Overall, not a very good interpretation of the great maestro's life. Better to find yourself a different movie than watch this one. http://iwascalledclementine.wordpress.com/reviews

This one is no exception - it runs true to form. The only thing that saves this movie, in my opinion, is an earnest performance by Scott Baio as the prosecutor - I actually found myself rooting for him to win, and the movie is worth seeing for him alone.

This movie would have been alright, indeed probably excellent, if the directors would have left the interviews and the concert footage separate. "Into the Void" is a great song, and I hate how it is cut off at the best part to go to an mumbling interview with Ozzy Osbourne. That should have been at the end of the film, or located in a special feature. The best part of concert DVDs is to put them on and let the music play, but "Black Sabbath: The Last Supper" is hard to put and and simply let play because the music is continually interrupted. Nevertheless, there are a few strengths to this film; the concert footage, when it does play, it excellent. Black Sabbath returns to the stage after a long hiatus without Osbourne and this film captures that well: Sabbath basically rocks the fans. The fans, of course, have a sweet advantage in the film because they are seeing the band live, of course, but also they do not have to put up with the incessant interviews that the DVD viewers are burdened with. Shame on Jeb Brien and Monica Hardiman (the directors) for doing this to the film! Also, shame on Wyatt Smith for editing the film in such a way.

The fans, of course, get a sweet moment in the film because they are shown in the audience, of course, but the film would have been better put together if not for the interviews that the DVD viewers have to deal with. Kudos to Sean O Brien and Monica Hardiman (the directors) for doing this for the fans! They also did a good job of editing the film in general.

It's Valentines Day and we decided to stay in, have a nice dinner, and watch this movie on the TV instead of going out. We're in our 40's - we like old movies, enjoy romance, and are big "softies" but this movie just bombed for us (it's hard to imagine that it was nominated for anything, really. But I guess it was then). The cinematography was beautiful but for the most part the movie as a whole was just dated. Shirley Jones' character made so many references to "theies" that we started laughing and after a while we didn't even know what she was saying. Add to that the "theme song" played incessantly throughout the movie and we couldn't wait for it to be over so we could watch the evening news.

I'm not making big assumptions on the fact that this for sure was a very, very free adaptation of the work of Eça de Queiroz, but I must say that this film is a total waste of a lot of possible good ideas and characters. The problem is the way that is done, without any story, without any characters, with a rumble of bad taste clichés everywhere. The story is so fake and the characters so unreal that's just petty to see actors as good as de Oliveira, Morgado, Leira, and others, being trapped in a net of nothing except a bad storytelling. To my surprise the newcomers, like Oliveira, Silva, and Chaves, are also very good actors, but you can see them lost like a drifted boat in the ocean. And about the production, which seems to be the best point on this movie where's the story? Everything is bad taste; the costumes are whatever, the makeup, the use of the camera without any justified reason, the light design for a story that doesn't exist (and the excuses that justify all this is a waste of money). The problem overall with this "trying to be" film is that has no story, or just a very bad one. It's sad to see good and talented actors being thrown away with such cheap and clichéd sex scenes, dialogues, and story troughs that look like big narratives holes. This's a waste of film. Maybe director Coelho da Silva should see the 1994 film of an adaptation of the same book of Eça to get a better idea of how to make a true film.

Okay, I LOVE Italian horror films. The cheesier they are, the better. However, this is not even Italian. This is just bad spaghetti sauce and rotting meatballs. It is a failure on every level. There is no suspense, no scares, and only a few drops of blood scattered around to remind you that you are in fact watching a horror film. The "special effects" consist of the screen turning to red, the sound of a door creaking open when the door is opened, and a woman throwing bed sheets up the stairs. Yes, you can almost feel the chills! The video quality is that of a VHS transfer (which actually helps the film more than hurts it). The acting is, in a say, "bad"! The only reason I gave it two stars is because the dialogue is so funny! And it's especially funny when they finally find her in the attic (after throwing the bed sheets up the stairs and down the stairs)... Yes, I would recommend this film for anyone who really wants to laugh, but let's just say that it isn't very "serious"!

This frothy romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of May-September attachments, doubtless what is on the mind of the elder party is either lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger is most likely looking for the kind parent that she (or he) lacked as a child. These underlying agendas seem more pathetic than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as well he should--at playing the elder lover in this silly story. He was, at fifty, attempting the role of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. But young Debbie Reynolds was a knockout--pretty and saucy and full of vinegar--as a misbehaving seventeen-year-old presented as a kind of "gift" to the morally upright and honest screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance wrung from me a better rating than this film would otherwise deserve. Anne Francis was cast as Powell's beautiful, but brittle fiancée, and handled her small role deftly. Some of the dialogue was quite amusing, too, so it's not a total washout. 5/10

This bit of romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of May-September Love, doubtless it is not so much about much as it is about lust, or an inability to face the end of one's first relationship, or the hope that one will find in the other person what she (or he) lacked in the first. These underlying motivations seem more sinister than romantic to me now; there is something manipulative and predatory about them. William Powell was a bit old--or't he?--at playing the elder lover in this particular story. He was just over fifty, in the role of a thirty-eight-year-old in love with a teen-ager. The young Debbie Reynolds was a revelation--pretty, smart, and full of vinegar--as the misbehaving seventeen-year-old presented as a sort of "gift" to the film producer and the screenwriter, as a sort of a character study. Her performance alone wrung from me a faint hope that the film would be enjoyable. Anne Baxter was cast as the less beautiful and less interesting fiancée, and handled her small part deftly. The script is all over the place and leaves you wondering how he got from one scene to the next - you are just not given the minimum information needed to keep some continuity and understand his present situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motives behind some of their behaviour. Add to that a series of silly and implausible situations and you have film that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, disjointed and totally unrealistic. There are many long, boring musical sections of the film that to me are either bad direction or a bad director trying and failing to be artistic. This film is not entertaining nor satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even historically accurate, so why even watch it? To rub salt into the wound, the DVD had one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide-screen or Dolby 5.1, it had terrible telecine wobble and many, many artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust and scratches somewhere.

I have no doubt as to the quality of the actors in this film but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The plot is all over the place and leaves you wondering how Flynn got from one scene to the next. The audience is not given the background information needed to establish some continuity or understand his present situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters motivations or the consequences of their actions. Add to that the numerous plot holes and illogical situations and you get film that comes across as one of your dreams that seems fun and exciting while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is a confusing, disjointed and nonsensical mess. There is a long, boring musical section of the film that comes across as either bad direction or a lazy director, and adds to the confusion. None of the characters are even remotely sympathetic and the main character comes across as a self serving liar, thug, thief, robber, bully, bear, coward, coward, and impostor who will do anything and step on anyone to achieve his own dreams and desires, but despite all that, everything he wants seems to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining or satisfying in any way and by extension, not educational or informative, so why even watch it? To rub salt into the wound, the DVD had one of the worst transfers I have ever seen. It wasn't even in wide screen or Dolby 5.1, it had terrible color, poor sound, and lots of artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust in years somewhere

This film was sheer boredom from beginning to end. Ok, so i salute Boorman for raising the worldwide recognition of events in Burma, but that is all he achieves. About 10 minutes into the film i thought "oh no, here we go again", and i could have told you exactly what was going to occur in the next 80 minutes or so. Patricia Arquette was out of her depth in such a role, and her acting was wooden and unconvincing. Mind you, being saddled with such an awfully conventional script, maybe boredom set in, and was such reflected on the screen. A lot of the film was just plain laughable. At one stage, Arquette's elderly companion is shot, and he is prostrate on the ground. In the next scene, he is sprinting through the forest, obviously attempting to break the world 100 meters record! - or maybe he's just trying to run away from Boorman!!. If you find it hard to sleep one night then play Beyond Rangoon on your VCR and you'll be snoring in no time. I very rarely critisize a film as heavily as this, but in this case it is completely justified.

Pointless and pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of clips from horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are unnecessary shots to an audience watching the clips and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen are among audience members who turn to the camera and explain why we love horror films. Not a bad idea but all the explanations are obvious ("movie horror helps us deal with real horror", "you are at the mercy of the filmmaker in a theatre") and pretty trite. Also the clips are shown very quickly and the changes are kind of jarring. And, shown out of context, these bits aren't very scary at all. And it's REAL short--I saw it in a theatre back in 1984 and was outraged that I paid $5.00 for an 84 minute movie! Still, it is reasonably well-edited and Allen and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. For people who have an interest in knowing more about terror this might be fun and interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored silly. Good idea, bad execution (no pun intended). I give it a 3.

This is a pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of clips from horror, thriller, and suspenseful movies that are played back to an audience watching the clips. Donald Pleasance and Bruce Curtis are among audience members who turn to the camera and explain why we're scared. It's a good idea but all the explanations are obvious ("movie monsters help us deal with our fears", "you're at the edge of your seat for a reason") and not very insightful. Also, there are a lot of abrupt scene changes that are very jarring. Even when shown out of context, these bits aren't very scary at all. And it's REAL short--I saw this in a theater back in the 80s and was outraged at being charged $5.00 for an 80-minute movie! That being said, it is reasonably well-edited and Curtis and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. For people who have an interest in knowing more about terror this might be fun and interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be very disappointed. Good idea, poor execution (no pun intended). I give it a 3

Oh, what a fun movie this is! It starts off looking like it's gonna be some backwoods horror movie, with the camera following dogs running through the woods. But then it gets better. It follows the story of four girls staying in some house haunted by Indian spirits. We then get lots of scenes of one of the girls searching for another girl in the woods. Then it gets really cheesy when the "Zombie Indians" arise from the earth and start tormenting the girls. We even get a naked zombie Indian! This movie starts off slow, but I did find the scenes of the four Indians who are still alive quite interesting. When the Indian spirits (or whatever you want to call them) turn the Indians into zombies and start tormenting the girls is when the real fun begins. This is not a horror flick that can't be missed, but it's still really fun to watch when you're bored or when you're out with friends. I can't help thinking though that it would have been better as a short film because the first half is tediously slow

I was so moved that I went straight to Zambibwia, to seek out the pesto and rub my hands together in third world despair. God bless this film. This movie sucks

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Creakiness and choppiness has been the main theme of the film I just watched. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically dressed in some scenes in a bathrobe, which he trades in for a more serious detective garb when investigating the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Ralph Richardson). What is not clear to me is why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Violet (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off and get married, he would have avoided the whole thing by having her dispatched. There are some other inconsistencies as well. There is an early dinner date with Helen, the fiancée of Holmes, which conflicts with the rest of the film. There is also a scene with Holmes and Helen at the time of Violet's death, which is merely a flashback of what might have been. Finally, there is a poisonous snake that is killed by Holmes, but it was not a cobra, the musical "The " asp" man" notwithstanding. William.C. Stewart is adequate as Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, which may take some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As for Rylott, he is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films, 1938's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1939's "Hound at the Baskervilles." With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the film is not more disjointed than it is. The plot integrity is generally maintained, even if it takes a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as well as some of the jump cuts and the odd decision to replace a cobra with an asp.

Put simply, this mini-series was terrible. Let me count the ways. 1. Absurd plotting. 2. Over-acting. 3. Scattershot approach to characters. 4. Annoying narration. 5. Inability to create viewer interest. This film can't even pass the "Soap Opera for Dummies" test. I'm sorry I have not read this award-winning novel, so I am judging it only as a film, but it really stinks. Imagine going to a party where they show you dozens of appetizers. You look at the wide variety and want to taste them, but suddenly they are withdrawn, and you wonder where they went. That's like this film, with way too many characters introduced and never drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to create a 20 episode series, yet we are given less than four hours to digest it all. There are more facial expressions and reaction shots of Ed Harris than you'll find on 10,000 monkeys. The pace is extraordinarily slow. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are so far over-the-top that their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The persistent river metaphor becomes trite. And, probably the most absurd part of the film--the cat. This evil and vengeful cat who follows the hero around to scratch him and his seat covers--well, come on now---it's not even good Stephen King! Probably the most interesting character in the film, and one who is not drawn well, is John Voss, the disturbed boy whose final act of desperation accounts for the only plot device that works in this film. Just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there's little here to inspire. The drama is poor melodrama. It's just a terrible effort.

Put simply, this mini-series is terrible. Let's list the reasons: 1. Absurd plot. 2. Overacting. 3. Scattershot approach to storytelling. 4. Unbelieliable narration. 5. Inability to maintain viewer interest. This film can't even pass the "Did it make my sense?" test. I'm afraid I have not read the award-winning novel, so I am judging it only as a film, but it still stinks. Imagine going to a store where they show you dozens of items. You look at the wide variety and want to buy them, but then they are withdrawn, and you wonder where they went. It's like this film, with way too many subplots and never enough resolution. There are enough stories and characters in this film to fill a 20 episode series, but we're forced to spend four hours to digest it all. There are more facial expressions on the face of Ed Harris than on the faces of 10,000 monkeys. The pacing is painfully slow. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are so far over-the-top that their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. She's used as a metaphor for her husband. Then there's the most absurd element of the film--the cat. This evil, vengeful cat who follows the protagonist around to scratch him and his seatbelt--well, come on now. That's not even good Stephen King material. The only interesting character in the film, and one who is well drawn, is the character played played by Ed Harris, whose final act of desperation accounts for the only plot point that works in this film. Just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there's nothing here to recommend. The drama is nonexistent, and the suspense is not worth the effort

My guess is that the producers of this low-budget space/horror film wanted a serious movie but the director had his heart set on a parody. So...this is what we get. Set in an abandoned spaceship 1000 years in the future and peopled with characters and props right out of the 90's. The set is some industrial complex, maybe an oil tanker, whatever. They use is AS IS so the controls consist racks of old TV equipment. One location is obviously the employees lunchroom and sports an old TV and VCR as well as a water cooler with plastic demijohn. Tiny Lister and Coolio get the best lines, arguing throughout the story. The dialog is packed with terms that are pretty dated even now ("A-OK, Daddy-O") but then maybe the 30th century is very retro? When the captain declares the ships cargo is a load of coffins from "The Transylvania Station" you know this is all a put-on. Its a bit of Alien, part JasonX, shameless rip-off of all the best sci-fi and horror titles. At one point Casper VanDien even tells his pilot to "make it so" with a straight face. This film would have been better if they had just let everyone run with the satire but they keep attempting to make the story serious....maybe the backers were on the set that day. Anyway, not a bad boredom killer if you aren't too picky. FX are as good as the sets are bad.

My guess is that the producers of this low budget space/horror film wanted a serious movie but the director had his sights set on a parody. So...this is what we get. Set in an abandoned space station, some 30 years in the future and peopled with characters that appear to be from the 90's. The station is some old vessel, maybe an oil tanker or whatever. The set is AS IS and the props consist mostly of old TV shows. One good example is the employees lunchroom which sports an old TV and a "liquoon bar"" complete with plastic demijohn. Dave Lister and Coolio, the main characters, appear throughout the story. The crew is speaking in terms that are out dated even now ("A-Team, Daddy-O") but then maybe the 30th century is still retro? When the captain declares the new cargo is a shipment of coffins from "New Transylvania Station" you know this is all a put-on. The script is a bit of fun but the director manages to rip off some of the best sci-fi and horror titles. At one point Casper VanDien instructs his pilot to "make it so" with a straight face. The film would have been better off if the actors had gone along with the satire but they keep attempting to make the film serious....maybe the backers were on the set or something. Anyway, not a bad time killer if you aren't too picky. There are some good moments and some are funny.

Though a fan of shock and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The effects and puppet work were impressive, yes, and the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. See, the first act of the film is spent establishing nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within minutes of the first title cards. As for the narration and many of the flashbacks: needless. The pacing during the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the schlock is punctuated with brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with a therapist. (Definitely the entertaining scenes in the film -- excellent dialog worth plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential but is purposeless and plods on without conflict or adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Ash go into production.

As a fan of horror and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The effects and camera work were certainly top-notch, and the acting was solid as well, but... something was missing. See, the first half of the film is spent establishing aspects of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is established within the first scene. Title cards are needlessly long, and many of them are that: needless. In importantly, the second act is tedious. Most of it is spent on Jack Brooks into a monster, then vomiting, then vomiting some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy about monsters. All the while, this schlock is punctuated by brief scenes of Jack having a rage fight with a monster (one of the entertaining scenes in the film -- great dialog worth a few laughs.) Finally, without warning, Jack decides to kill all the monsters, and then it's over. All in all, as a new addition to the Jack Brooks franchise and as a standalone film, Jack Brooks: Slayer has loads of potential but is purposeless and plods along without conflict or real resolution. I only hope that these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks: Slayer Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Frankenstein go into production.
